hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 adheres more tightly to some recycling receptors than APOE3, impeding recycling.

rows.Finding description: Without insulin, nearly 20% of IR-GFP colocalized with transferrin-positive endosomes after apoE4, with less colocalization after apoE3, across three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: In the absence of insulin, we found that nearly 20% of IR-GFP co-localized with transferrin in the endosomal compartment in apoE4-treated cells whereas less co-localization was observed in apoE3-treated cells (Figures 6A and 6D).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (greater insulin-receptor localization in transferrin-positive endosomes)
rows.Experimental system: Human SH-SY5Y cells expressing human IR-GFP; overnight 100 nM recombinant apoE, no insulin; Alexa568-transferrin at 20 μg/ml for one hour; confocal colocalization analysis.

rows.Finding description: Thirty minutes into the recycling assay, apoE4-pretreated neurons retained significantly more intracellular insulin receptor than apoE3-pretreated neurons.
rows.Finding quote: Intriguingly, significantly higher amount of intracellular IR was detected in apoE4-treated cells compared with cells treated with apoE3 at 30 minutes and 60 minutes, indicating that apoE4 impaired IR recycling (Figure S8B).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (impaired insulin-receptor recycling at 30 minutes)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical Apoe−/− mouse neurons; cleavable surface biotin, 100 nM recombinant apoE for 30 minutes to load internalized receptors, apoE removal, then recycling at 37°C and a second surface-biotin stripping step.

rows.Finding description: Astrocyte-secreted lipidated apoE4 particles bound insulin receptor more strongly than lipidated apoE3 particles in three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: Similar to recombinant apoE, we found that apoE4 lipoprotein particles bind to IR more strongly than apoE3 lipoprotein particles (Figure 5B).
rows.Finding summary: (lipidated apoE3 -> lipidated apoE4) -> (stronger binding to insulin receptor)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free solid-phase assay using human apoE3 or apoE4 lipoprotein particles purified from immortalized astrocytes derived from human apoE-targeted-replacement mice, and recombinant human insulin receptor.

rows.Finding description: Without insulin, approximately 15% of IR-GFP was intracellular with apoE3 versus nearly 40% with apoE4 in three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: In the absence of insulin, the majority of the IR-GFP was localized to the cell membrane with only 15% of the receptor localized intracellularly in apoE3-treated cells (Figures 6A–C). Interestingly, nearly 40% of IR-GFP was localized in the intracellular compartment in apoE4-treated cells (Figures 6A–C), consistent with our observation in which apoE4 reduced cell surface IR (Figures 5G–I).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (greater intracellular insulin-receptor localization)
rows.Experimental system: Human SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma neuronal cells expressing transfected human IR-GFP; overnight 100 nM recombinant apoE3 or apoE4, without insulin; confocal microscopy with transferrin labeling.

rows.Finding description: Insulin increased IR-GFP colocalization with transferrin after apoE3 treatment but produced no significant increase after apoE4 treatment in three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: Insulin induced IR internalization which increased the co-localization of IR-GFP with transferrin in apoE3-treated cells, but not in apoE4-treated cells (Figures 6A and 6D).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (reduced insulin-induced increase in endosomal insulin receptor)
rows.Experimental system: Human SH-SY5Y cells expressing human IR-GFP; overnight 100 nM recombinant apoE, transferrin labeling for one hour, and 100 nM insulin during the final 30 minutes; confocal microscopy.

rows.Finding description: Surface-biotinylation immunoblots showed no significant difference in neuronal surface LRP1 after apoE3 versus apoE4 treatment.
rows.Finding quote: No significant differences were found in the levels of cell surface and total LRP1, NMDAR, AMPAR, and Na-K-ATPase after apoE3 and apoE4 treatments (Figures S7A, C–F, H–K).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in neuronal surface LRP1)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from embryonic Apoe−/− mice treated with recombinant apoE isoforms; cell-surface biotinylation and LRP1 immunoblotting.

rows.Finding description: At 60 minutes, apoE4-treated neurons retained significantly more internalized insulin receptor than apoE3-treated neurons, indicating delayed receptor recycling.
rows.Finding quote: After 60 minutes treatment with apoE3, the amount of internalized (biotinylated) IR was reduced, reflecting a membrane recycling of IR and subsequent biotin cleavage. Interestingly, apoE4-treated cells exhibited significantly more intracellular IR compared to those treated with apoE3 at 60 minutes, suggesting a delayed recycling of IR in the presence of apoE4 (Figure S8A).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (greater intracellular insulin-receptor retention at 60 minutes)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from embryonic Apoe−/− mice; surface proteins labeled with cleavable biotin at 4°C, then 100 nM recombinant apoE at 37°C; surface stripping and intracellular insulin-receptor immunoblotting.

rows.Finding description: After insulin-induced internalization, intracellular insulin receptor declined with apoE3 but showed no obvious decline with apoE4, consistent with impaired recycling.
rows.Finding quote: In the presence of apoE3, the plateau of the curve shifted to 15 minutes and then started to decline (Figure S9). However, in the presence of apoE4, the internalization of IR did not approach plateau until 30 minutes and without obvious decline over time (Figure S9), indicating that apoE4 inhibited insulin-induced IR trafficking.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (reduced post-internalization loss of intracellular insulin receptor)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical Apoe−/− mouse neurons; cleavable surface biotin, 100 nM insulin with 100 nM recombinant apoE, incubation at 37°C, surface stripping and intracellular receptor immunoblot time course.

rows.Finding description: Recombinant apoE4 bound insulin receptor with higher affinity than recombinant apoE3 in three independent solid-phase binding experiments.
rows.Finding quote: Conversely, we found that both recombinant apoE3 and apoE4 specifically bound to IR with apoE4 having higher binding affinity than apoE3 (Figure 5A).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (higher binding affinity for insulin receptor)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free assay using recombinant human apoE isoforms and human insulin receptor; apoE immobilized at 400 ng/well, receptor binding measured after 24 hours at 4°C; one-site binding curves.

rows.Finding description: More insulin receptor co-immunoprecipitated with recombinant apoE4 than with recombinant apoE3 after solution incubation.
rows.Finding quote: We found that more IR was co-immunoprecipitated with apoE4 than with apoE3 (Figure 5C).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (greater insulin-receptor association)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free solution binding of recombinant human apoE at 1 μM and human insulin receptor at 400 nM for one hour at 37°C, followed by apoE immunoprecipitation and insulin-receptor immunoblotting.

rows.Finding description: Insulin increased intracellular IR-GFP after apoE3 treatment but produced no significant increase after apoE4 treatment in three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: Importantly, insulin stimulation increased the percentage of intracellular IR-GFP in apoE3-treated, but not in apoE4-treated, cells (Figures 6A–C).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (reduced insulin-induced increase in intracellular insulin receptor)
rows.Experimental system: Human SH-SY5Y cells transfected with human IR-GFP; overnight 100 nM recombinant apoE followed by 100 nM insulin for 30 minutes; confocal microscopy.

rows.Finding description: Without insulin stimulation, apoE4 reduced neuronal surface insulin receptor relative to apoE3 in three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: In the absence of insulin stimulation, we found that apoE4 but not apoE3 significantly reduced the amount of cell surface IR (Figures 5G, H).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (lower neuronal surface insulin receptor)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from embryonic day 16–18 Apoe−/− mice, cultured to DIV10, treated overnight with 100 nM recombinant human apoE; surface biotinylation and insulin-receptor immunoblotting without insulin.

rows.Finding description: Insulin internalized approximately 50% of total insulin receptor after apoE3 treatment versus approximately 20% after apoE4 treatment in three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: Importantly, ~50% of the total IR was internalized in response to insulin in apoE3-treated cells, whereas only ~20% of IR was internalized in apoE4-treated cells upon insulin stimulation (Figure 5I).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (less insulin-induced insulin-receptor internalization)
rows.Experimental system: DIV10 primary cortical neurons from embryonic Apoe−/− mice; overnight 100 nM recombinant human apoE isoforms followed by 100 nM insulin for 30 minutes; changes in surface-biotinylated insulin receptor.

rows.Finding description: Surface-biotinylation immunoblots showed lower neuronal surface insulin receptor after apoE4 than apoE3 treatment.
rows.Finding quote: As expected, cell surface IR was decreased after treatment with apoE4 compared with apoE3 (Figures S7A, B) without affecting the total IR (Figures S7A, G).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (lower neuronal surface insulin receptor)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from embryonic Apoe−/− mice treated with recombinant apoE isoforms; cell-surface biotinylation followed by surface and total protein immunoblotting.

rows.Finding description: At 16 μg/ml, apoE4 inhibited insulin–insulin-receptor binding by nearly 50%, versus 25% with apoE3, in three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: When apoE was co-incubated with insulin and IR, we found that apoE4 (16 μg/ml) reduced insulin-IR binding by nearly 50%, which is significantly higher than apoE3 treatment (25%) (Figure 5F).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (greater inhibition of insulin binding to insulin receptor)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free competition assay with recombinant human apoE, biotinylated human insulin at 8 nM and human insulin receptor at 80 nM; one-hour incubation at 37°C followed by streptavidin capture.

rows.Finding description: ApoE3 and apoE4 produced no significant difference in IR-GFP colocalization with lysosomes, with or without insulin, in three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: No differences were observed for the co-localization of IR-GFP with Lysotracker, a lysosomal marker, between apoE3- and apoE4-treated cells, with or without insulin (Figures 6B and 6E).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no significant difference detected in lysosomal insulin-receptor localization)
rows.Experimental system: Human SH-SY5Y cells expressing human IR-GFP; overnight 100 nM recombinant apoE; 10 μM Lysotracker for one hour, with or without 100 nM insulin for 30 minutes; confocal microscopy.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 undergoes increased aggregation in the endo-lysosome compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: APOE4–mCh showed significantly greater colocalization with LAMP1-marked lysosomes than APOE3–mCh in human HEK293 cells, using three wells per isoform.
rows.Finding quote: Imaris analysis revealed that APOE4–mCh cells had significantly higher colocalization between APOE and lysosomes, and significantly greater average surface area of individual lysosomal and APOE puncta (Fig. 3A) than did APOE3–mCh cells, suggesting greater trafficking to lysosomes.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (greater APOE–lysosome colocalization)
rows.Experimental system: Human HEK293 cells, ATCC CRL-1573; stable APOE3–mCherry versus APOE4–mCherry expression; transient CellLight LAMP1–GFP lysosomal labeling; live confocal microscopy and Imaris colocalization analysis; three images per well.

rows.Finding description: Dual-tagged APOE4 produced a significantly lower green-to-red fluorescence ratio than APOE3 in human HEK293 cells, indicating greater acidic lysosomal localization using three wells per isoform.
rows.Finding quote: APOE4–mCh–SepH cells had a significantly lower ratio of green to red fluorescence compared with APOE3–mCh–SepH cells, indicating a greater degree of lysosomal localization of the protein (Fig. 3B).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower green-to-red reporter ratio, indicating greater lysosomal APOE localization)
rows.Experimental system: Human HEK293 cells, ATCC CRL-1573; stable expression of APOE3–mCherry–SepHluorin versus APOE4–mCherry–SepHluorin; live confocal imaging and Imaris fluorescence-area analysis; three images per well. Acid-sensitive SepHluorin is quenched in acidic compartments.

rows.Finding description: After uptake into rat ST14A cells, APOE4 showed significantly greater colocalization with late than early endosomes whereas APOE3 did not, using three wells per genotype without a reported direct between-isoform significance test.
rows.Finding quote: APOE4 colocalized with late endosomes significantly more than with early endosomes, whereas APOE3 did not.
rows.Finding summary: (extracellular APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (late-over-early endosomal localization preference observed for APOE4)
rows.Experimental system: Immortalized rat neuron-like ST14A cells; 24 h exposure to conditioned medium containing human APOE3–mCherry or APOE4–mCherry; fixed-cell staining for mCherry and early-endosomal EEA1 or late-endosomal Rab7; confocal imaging and Imaris colocalization analysis.

rows.Finding description: During bafilomycin treatment, APOE4–mCh fluorescence increased more strongly over time than APOE3–mCh fluorescence in human HEK293 cells, with four wells per treatment.
rows.Finding quote: There was a significant difference between slopes of APOE3–mCh and APOE4–mCh fluorescence treated with Baf over time when analyzed by linear regression, suggesting that APOE4–mCh fluorescence is more strongly affected by Baf and is turned over more rapidly by the lysosome.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (greater fluorescence accumulation during lysosomal inhibition)
rows.Experimental system: Human HEK293 cells, ATCC CRL-1573; stable clonal APOE3–mCherry versus APOE4–mCherry expression; bafilomycin A1 treatment, 50 nM; live-cell fluorescence time course and linear-regression comparison of slopes. The figure legend specifies a 4 h treatment.

rows.Finding description: Rat neuron-like ST14A cells accumulated more intracellular red fluorescence from APOE4–mCh than APOE3–mCh conditioned medium during the uptake time course, using three wells per medium genotype.
rows.Finding quote: Internalization levels were isoform-dependent, with the highest fluorescence observed in both cell types treated with APOE4–mCh, and the lowest in APOE2–mCh-treated cells (Fig. 7A,B).
rows.Finding summary: (extracellular APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher intracellular APOE-associated fluorescence during uptake)
rows.Experimental system: Immortalized rat neuronally derived ST14A cells, supplied by Elena Cattaneo's laboratory; no endogenous APOE detected by western blot; human HEK293T conditioned medium containing APOE3–mCherry or APOE4–mCherry, mixed 1:1 with fresh medium; IncuCyte fluorescence normalized to phase area over time. Endpoint duration is not stated in the supplied Fig 7B text.

rows.Finding description: In human HEK293 cells, APOE4–mCh had significantly higher whole-cell protein abundance than APOE3–mCh, measured using four wells per genotype.
rows.Finding quote: APOE4–mCh cells have significantly higher APOE levels by western blot (Fig. 1A) and fluorescence (Fig. 2) than APOE3–mCh, in spite of similar APOE RNA levels (Fig. S1Ai).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher intracellular APOE protein abundance)
rows.Experimental system: Human embryonic kidney HEK293 cells, ATCC CRL-1573; one selected stable clonal line per APOE–mCherry construct; baseline whole-cell western blotting. These are not brain cells; no aging or AD model was specified.

rows.Finding description: Bafilomycin significantly increased APOE4–mCh protein abundance in human HEK293 cells, testing lysosomal degradation within a fixed APOE4 background using three wells per treatment.
rows.Finding quote: Baf treatment significantly increased the abundance of APOE3–mCh and APOE4–mCh (Fig. 1B), and red fluorescence of APOE3–mCh and APOE4–mCh cells (Fig. 2).
rows.Finding summary: (lysosomal inhibition in APOE4 cells) -> (higher intracellular APOE4 protein abundance)
rows.Experimental system: Human HEK293 cells, ATCC CRL-1573, stably expressing APOE4–mCherry; bafilomycin A1, 50 nM for 4 h, versus untreated cells; whole-cell western blotting.

rows.Finding description: APOE4–mCh-expressing human HEK293 cells had significantly higher baseline red fluorescence than APOE3–mCh cells, with four wells per treatment.
rows.Finding quote: APOE4–mCh cells have significantly higher APOE levels by western blot (Fig. 1A) and fluorescence (Fig. 2) than APOE3–mCh, in spite of similar APOE RNA levels (Fig. S1Ai).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher intracellular APOE-associated fluorescence)
rows.Experimental system: Human HEK293 cells, ATCC CRL-1573; stable clonal APOE3–mCherry versus APOE4–mCherry expression; live-cell fluorescence imaging. Fluorescence measures intracellular abundance, not an aggregate-specific signal.

rows.Finding description: Bafilomycin significantly increased intracellular APOE4–mCh red fluorescence in human HEK293 cells, testing lysosomal degradation within a fixed APOE4 background using four wells per treatment.
rows.Finding quote: Baf treatment significantly increased the abundance of APOE3–mCh and APOE4–mCh (Fig. 1B), and red fluorescence of APOE3–mCh and APOE4–mCh cells (Fig. 2).
rows.Finding summary: (lysosomal inhibition in APOE4 cells) -> (higher intracellular APOE4-associated fluorescence)
rows.Experimental system: Human HEK293 cells, ATCC CRL-1573, stably expressing APOE4–mCherry; bafilomycin A1, 50 nM, versus untreated cells; live-cell fluorescence imaging. The figure legend specifies a 4 h treatment.

rows.Finding description: Rapamycin significantly increased APOE4–mCh protein abundance in human HEK293 cells, testing autophagy modulation within a fixed APOE4 background using three wells per treatment.
rows.Finding quote: Whereas Rap treatment significantly increased the LC3II/LC3I ratio (Fig. 1B), suggesting that LC3-dependent autophagy was effectively stimulated, Rap did not significantly reduce APOE levels. Instead, the abundance of APOE4–mCh significantly increased (Fig. 1B).
rows.Finding summary: (rapamycin treatment in APOE4 cells) -> (higher intracellular APOE4 protein abundance)
rows.Experimental system: Human HEK293 cells, ATCC CRL-1573, stably expressing APOE4–mCherry; rapamycin, 10 nM for 4 h, versus untreated cells; whole-cell western blotting.

rows.Finding description: After uptake into rat ST14A cells, 22% of LC3A/B spots colocalized with APOE4 versus 17% with APOE3, using four wells per genotype; between-isoform significance was not reported.
rows.Finding quote: Colocalization of APOE with LC3A and/or LC3B was observed, with 17% of LC3A and LC3B spots colocalizing with APOE3–mCh and 22% colocalizing with APOE4–mCH spots (Fig. S8C).
rows.Finding summary: (extracellular APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher reported fraction of LC3A/B spots colocalizing with APOE)
rows.Experimental system: Immortalized rat neuron-like ST14A cells; 24 h exposure to conditioned medium containing human APOE3–mCherry or APOE4–mCherry; endogenous LC3A/B and mCherry immunostaining; confocal microscopy and Imaris spot analysis, defining colocalization by centers within 1 μm; four images per well. LC3 association does not establish lysosomal localization or APOE aggregation.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Fig S8C; Supplementary Table S5

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 adheres more tightly to some recycling receptors than APOE3, impeding recycling.

rows.Finding description: The modeled stable LDLR complex dissociated more slowly for fasting APOE3/E4 VLDL1-rich particles than APOE3/E3 particles, with kd2 values of 9.7 versus 11.2 × 10−4 s−1.
rows.Finding quote: Relative to the APOE3/E3 group, the dissociation rate constant (kd2) was lower (P = 0.013) and overall K2 was higher (P = 0.032) for the second step of the binding of fasting APOE3/E4 VLDL1-rich particles to the LDLR.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3/E3 -> APOE3/E4) -> (slower stable VLDL1-LDLR complex dissociation)
rows.Experimental system: Fasting human male plasma VLDL1-rich TRL, Sf 60–400, pooled from two subjects per sample; trial mean age 48 ± 16 years. LDLR ectodomain SPR, 5 nM apoB, 25 °C, two-state fit; no endosomal pH or recycling assay.

rows.Finding description: Fasting VLDL1-rich particles from APOE3/E4 and APOE3/E3 men showed no significant difference in overall LDLR binding affinity.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3/E3 -> APOE3/E4) -> (no change in overall VLDL1-LDLR binding affinity)
rows.Experimental system: Fasting human male plasma VLDL1-rich TRL, Sf 60–400, pooled from two subjects per sample; LDLR ectodomain SPR, 5 nM apoB, 25 °C, two-state fit. No receptor recycling measured.

rows.Finding description: Fasting VLDL2-rich particles from APOE3/E4 and APOE3/E3 men showed no significant difference in stable LDLR-complex dissociation rate.
rows.Finding quote: There were no significant genotype effects observed for the binding of the fasting VLDL2-rich fraction (Table 1), nor on the apoE content of either fasting TRL fraction estimated using the apoE/apoB ratio.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3/E3 -> APOE3/E4) -> (no change in stable VLDL2-LDLR complex dissociation rate)
rows.Experimental system: Fasting human male plasma VLDL2-rich TRL, Sf 20–60, pooled from two subjects per sample; LDLR ectodomain SPR, 5 nM apoB, 25 °C, two-state fit. No receptor recycling measured.

rows.Finding description: Postprandial VLDL1-rich particles from APOE3/E4 and APOE3/E3 men showed no significant genotype effect or meal-by-genotype interaction on LDLR binding; genotype-specific values were not presented.
rows.Finding quote: There were no significant genotype or meal*genotype interactions observed for the binding of postprandial TRL fractions to the LDLR.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3/E3 -> APOE3/E4) -> (no change in postprandial VLDL1-LDLR binding)
rows.Experimental system: Human male crossover trial; VLDL1-rich TRL sampled at individual apoB/apoE peaks, usually 240–360 minutes after SFA, SFA-FO or UNSAT meals; two-subject pools. LDLR ectodomain SPR, 5 nM apoB, 25 °C; no recycling assay.
rows.Data location: Results, 'APOE genotype and the binding of postprandial TRL fractions to the LDLR', first sentence; Table 2 presents genotype-combined meal effects

rows.Finding description: Fasting VLDL1-rich particles from APOE3/E4 and APOE3/E3 men showed no significant difference in initial LDLR-complex dissociation rate.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3/E3 -> APOE3/E4) -> (no change in initial VLDL1-LDLR dissociation rate)
rows.Experimental system: Fasting human male plasma VLDL1-rich TRL, Sf 60–400, pooled from two subjects per sample; LDLR ectodomain SPR, 5 nM apoB, 25 °C, two-state fit. No receptor recycling measured.

rows.Finding description: Fasting VLDL1-rich particles from APOE3/E4 and APOE3/E3 men showed no significant difference in the initial LDLR equilibrium binding constant.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3/E3 -> APOE3/E4) -> (no change in initial VLDL1-LDLR equilibrium binding constant)
rows.Experimental system: Fasting human male plasma VLDL1-rich TRL, Sf 60–400, pooled from two subjects per sample; LDLR ectodomain SPR, 5 nM apoB, 25 °C, two-state fit. No receptor recycling measured.

rows.Finding description: Fasting VLDL1-rich particles from APOE3/E4 and APOE3/E3 men showed no significant difference in modeled stable LDLR-complex formation rate.
rows.Finding quote: However, in our study, a similar ka2 constant was observed for both fasting LDL and TRL isolated from the APOE3/E3 and APOE3/E4 groups, suggesting that the higher binding affinity in APOE4 carriers may reflect the conformation of APOE4 on the surface of these particles which, due to the lower stability of the helix bundle, binds to the receptor in the open conformation.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3/E3 -> APOE3/E4) -> (no change in VLDL1-LDLR stable-complex formation rate)
rows.Experimental system: Fasting human male plasma VLDL1-rich TRL, Sf 60–400, pooled from two subjects per sample; LDLR ectodomain SPR, 5 nM apoB, 25 °C, two-state fit. No receptor recycling measured.

rows.Finding description: Fasting VLDL1-rich particles from APOE3/E4 men initially associated with LDLR more slowly than APOE3/E3 particles, with ka1 values of 9.3 versus 11.3 × 10^5 M−1s−1.
rows.Finding quote: A slower association rate was also observed with the fasting VLDL1-rich particles from the APOE3/E4 group, but once the VLDL1-LDLR complex was formed, it was found to be more stable and dissociated at a slower rate than the APOE3/E3 VLDL-1 rich fraction.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3/E3 -> APOE3/E4) -> (slower initial VLDL1-LDLR association)
rows.Experimental system: Fasting human male plasma VLDL1-rich TRL, Sf 60–400, pooled from two subjects per sample; trial mean age 48 ± 16 years. LDLR ectodomain SPR, 5 nM apoB, 25 °C, two-state fit; no brain cells or recycling assay.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 undergoes increased aggregation in the endo-lysosome compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: A2E plus complement exposure increased the fraction of large apoE3 condensates but produced no stress-induced increase in apoE4 condensates in primary porcine RPE, opposing greater stress-induced condensation of apoE4; 15–29 cells were analyzed per condition.
rows.Finding quote: We also observed a small but significant increase in large condensates in ApoE3-RPE exposed to A2E and NHS, whereas ApoE4-RPE were completely resistant to this stress-induced phase separation (Figure 5A).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (resistance to stress-induced enlargement of intracellular apoE condensates)
rows.Experimental system: Primary adult porcine RPE monolayers expressing human mCherry-tagged apoE3 or apoE4; A2E treatment at 10 μM for 6 hours followed by a 48-hour chase, with normal human serum as a complement source. Live confocal imaging and 3D reconstruction measured the percentage of apoE condensates exceeding 0.6 μm3. Endo-lysosomal localization was not established.

rows.Finding description: Baseline apoE4 condensates had a higher printed mean volume than apoE3 condensates in primary porcine RPE, 0.3233 versus 0.2596 μm3, respectively; the printed medians were also higher, 0.15 versus 0.12 μm3, but comparative significance was not reported.
rows.Finding quote: N/A
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (higher baseline mean intracellular apoE condensate volume)
rows.Experimental system: Primary adult porcine RPE monolayers transiently expressing human mCherry-tagged apoE3 or apoE4; baseline live confocal imaging and 3D surface reconstruction, with condensate-volume histograms generated in Matlab. These are intracellular condensates without demonstrated endo-lysosomal localization, not human brain-cell aggregates.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Fig S4E, ApoE3 histogram; Supplementary Fig S4F, ApoE4 histogram

rows.Finding description: The reported significant large-condensate comparisons were ApoE2 versus ApoE3 or ApoE4. For ApoE4 versus ApoE3, the companion histograms show descriptively higher mean and median baseline volumes, with no reported pairwise significance.
rows.Finding quote: Although the 3 isoforms had similar disorder tendencies when analyzed by meta-predictors such as DisMeta (49) and other commonly used disorder predictors (Supplemental Figure 4, A–C), there were significantly more ApoE2 condensates with larger volumes (>0.6 μm3), compared with either ApoE3 or ApoE4 condensates (Figure 4D and Supplemental Figure 4, D–F).
rows.Finding summary: ApoE4 had higher descriptive mean and median baseline condensate volumes than ApoE3. The fraction above 0.6 μm³ has no stated ApoE4-versus-ApoE3 result.
rows.Experimental system: Primary adult porcine RPE monolayers transiently expressing human mCherry-tagged apoE3 or apoE4; baseline live confocal imaging, Imaris 3D surface reconstruction and condensate-volume frequency distributions. No endosomal or lysosomal markers were used for this readout.
rows.Data location: Fig 4D for volume-frequency distributions and sample-size range; Supplementary Fig S4E–F for ApoE3 and ApoE4 means and medians

rows.Finding description: Live imaging showed that both human apoE3 and apoE4 formed spherical intracellular condensate-like structures in primary porcine RPE, without establishing an apoE4-versus-apoE3 difference in aggregation in this panel.
rows.Finding quote: Live-cell imaging showed that ApoE forms spherical structures with average sphericity approximately 0.9 (Figure 4, A and B) that readily fuse and relax (Figure 4C), suggesting that ApoE2, ApoE3, and ApoE4 all segregate into liquid-like assemblies within the RPE.
rows.Finding summary: Intracellular condensates were visible with both ApoE3 and ApoE4. This shared presence gives no direction for a difference in aggregation burden.
rows.Experimental system: Primary adult porcine retinal pigment epithelial cells isolated from freshly harvested eyes, plated as confluent monolayers and transiently expressing human mCherry-tagged apoE3 or apoE4; imaged 48–72 hours after transfection by live spinning-disc confocal microscopy with 3D surface reconstruction. No endosomal or lysosomal localization was established, and these were not human brain cells.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 adheres more tightly to some recycling receptors than APOE3, impeding recycling.

rows.Finding description: Across three independent experiments in primary mouse neurons treated with Reelin, human ApoE4 reduced surface ApoER2 more than ApoE3.
rows.Finding quote: Receptor surface levels show a stronger reduction with ApoE4 than ApoE3.
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (lower neuronal surface ApoER2 during Reelin stimulation)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons isolated from E18 Slc9a6 wildtype mouse embryos, with female Slc9a6+/+ and male Slc9a6y/+ littermates represented; no AD-model mutation reported for this assay. At DIV10–14, neurons received human ApoE3 or ApoE4 conditioned medium from transfected HEK293 cells, 5 μg/ml for 30 minutes, followed by Reelin, 2 μg/ml for another 30 minutes. Surface ApoER2 was measured by sulfo-NHS-SS-biotin labeling, NeutrAvidin isolation, and immunoblotting, with total receptor immunoblots. This measures receptor surface availability as a recycling readout, not apoE binding strength or dissociation kinetics; the brain cells were mouse, not human.

rows.Finding description: Across three independent experiments in primary mouse neurons treated with Reelin, adding human ApoE4 reduced surface ApoER2 compared with the condition without added apoE.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE-conditioned media treatment reduces the surface expression of Apoer2 and glutamate receptors in presence of Reelin in primary neurons. Receptor surface levels show a stronger reduction with ApoE4 than ApoE3.
rows.Finding summary: (No added apoE -> added ApoE4) -> (lower neuronal surface ApoER2 during Reelin stimulation)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from E18 Slc9a6 wildtype mouse embryos, assayed at DIV10–14; no AD-model mutation reported. Human ApoE4 was supplied in HEK293 conditioned medium at 5 μg/ml for 30 minutes before a further 30-minute Reelin treatment at 2 μg/ml; the comparator lacked added apoE. Surface ApoER2 was measured by surface biotinylation, NeutrAvidin isolation, and immunoblotting. The endpoint assesses surface availability associated with recycling, without measuring receptor–apoE binding or dissociation; these were mouse brain cells.

rows.Finding description: Across three independent experiments, germline NHE6 deletion completely restored the ApoER2 recycling readout in primary mouse neurons exposed to human ApoE4 and Reelin.
rows.Finding quote: Apoer2 recycling was completely restored in Slc9a6- neurons treated with ApoE4 (Figure 4C).
rows.Finding summary: (NHE6 present -> NHE6 deleted, with ApoE4) -> (restored neuronal surface ApoER2)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from E18 germline Slc9a6-knockout mouse embryos and wildtype littermates, including female Slc9a6-/- and male Slc9a6y/- knockouts; no AD-model mutation reported. At DIV10–14, cultures received HEK293-secreted human ApoE4 at 5 μg/ml for 30 minutes, followed by Reelin at 2 μg/ml for another 30 minutes. Surface biotinylation and immunoblotting quantified ApoER2 surface availability. Endosomal pH and apoE–receptor binding were not measured in this neuronal panel; the cells were mouse, not human.

rows.Finding description: Across three independent experiments, germline NHE6 deletion restored ApoE4-impaired surface GluN2B expression in primary mouse neurons treated with Reelin.
rows.Finding quote: In addition, genetic loss of NHE6 equally restored the ApoE4-impaired surface expression of AMPA and NMDA receptor subunits (Figure 4D–F).
rows.Finding summary: (NHE6 present -> NHE6 deleted, with ApoE4) -> (restored neuronal surface GluN2B)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from E18 germline Slc9a6-knockout mouse embryos and wildtype littermates, assayed at DIV10–14; no AD-model mutation reported. Human ApoE4 from HEK293 conditioned medium was applied at 5 μg/ml for 30 minutes, followed by Reelin at 2 μg/ml for another 30 minutes. Surface GluN2B was measured by biotinylation and immunoblotting. This tests rescue of co-trafficked receptor surface availability in mouse neurons, without measuring apoE–receptor binding or neuronal endosomal pH.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 undergoes increased aggregation in the endo-lysosome compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: Native PAGE supported greater aggregation of lipid-free recombinant human ApoE4 than ApoE3; data represent two independently prepared ApoE isoform samples.
rows.Finding quote: Together, these results suggest that lipid‐free ApoE has the tendency to aggregate in solution at a concentration of 0.1 mg·mL−1, whereas lipidation is capable of impeding this behavior. This tendency is isoform dependent, with the most pronounced aggregation for ApoE4, followed by ApoE3 and ApoE2 (Fig. 3).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (greater lipid-free apoE aggregation in vitro)
rows.Experimental system: Commercial recombinant human ApoE3 and ApoE4 from Leinco Technologies, lipid-free at 0.1 mg·mL−1 in PBS; native 4–20% Tris-glycine PAGE, with 3 μg ApoE loaded and electrophoresis at 4 °C for 16 h. Cell-free; no endo-lysosomal localization or acidic-pH condition.

rows.Finding description: FFF refractive-index profiles contributed to the authors' conclusion that lipid-free recombinant human ApoE4 self-assembled more than ApoE3; profiles represent two independently prepared ApoE isoform samples.
rows.Finding quote: Our results show that lipid‐free ApoE has the tendency to self‐assemble, with ApoE4 having the highest aggregation propensity, followed by ApoE3 and ApoE2 (Figs 2, 3, 4).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (greater lipid-free apoE self-assembly in vitro)
rows.Experimental system: Commercial recombinant human ApoE3 and ApoE4 from Leinco Technologies, lipid-free at 0.1 mg·mL−1 in PBS; asymmetrical flow field flow fractionation with differential refractive-index detection. Cell-free, without endosomes or lysosomes; no acidic-pH experiment or aggregation time course reported.
rows.Data location: Fig 2A; Discussion sentence attributing the isoform-dependent self-assembly ranking to Figs 2, 3, 4

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 adheres more tightly to some recycling receptors than APOE3, impeding recycling.

rows.Finding description: In normal human fibroblasts, DMPC-apoE4 produced 50% inhibition of LDL binding at 0.036 μg/ml versus 0.039 μg/ml for DMPC-apoE3, indicating slightly stronger competition without a reported significance test.
rows.Finding quote: Competition curves comparing LDLR binding by LDL ( Figure 7A ) and dimyristoyl phosphatidylcholine (DMPC) vesicles ( Figure 7B ) indicate that both LDL and DMPC vesicles exhibit a clear dose response, with 50% binding inhibition at 3.44 μg/ml for LDL, and 0.039 and 0.036 μg/ml for E3-DMPC and E4-DMPC, respectively.
rows.Finding summary: (DMPC-apoE3 -> DMPC-apoE4) -> (lower concentration required for 50% inhibition of LDLR binding)
rows.Experimental system: Normal human fibroblasts cultured for one week before binding assays; donor age and tissue source unspecified. Recombinant human apoE3 or apoE4 was mixed with DMPC at 1:3.75 protein:lipid by weight. Cells were incubated for 2 hours at 4°C with 2 μg/ml radiolabeled human LDL and varying competitor concentrations. LDL binding was measured in triplicate.

rows.Finding description: Radiolabeled HEK-secreted apoE4 showed similar single-cycle trafficking kinetics to apoE3 in wild-type mouse fibroblasts; no significant difference was reported, although no isoform statistical test or receptor-recycling measurement was provided.
rows.Finding quote: When 125 I-apoE4 was used in the single-cycle endocytosis assay, similar kinetics were observed ( Figure 8B ).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in reported single-cycle apoE trafficking kinetics)
rows.Experimental system: Wild-type mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEF-1), expressing LRP and LDLR; mouse age and background unspecified. SEC-isolated, virtually lipid-free human HEK-293-secreted radiolabeled apoE3 or apoE4 was bound at 5 nM for 1.5 hours at 4°C, washed, and chased at 37°C with RAP. The legend specifies 500 nM RAP, whereas Methods and Results specify 1 μM. Pronase distinguished surface-bound from internalized ligand; medium TCA precipitation distinguished dissociated from degraded ligand. Time courses extended to 2.5 hours, with triplicate determinations.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 undergoes increased aggregation in the endo-lysosome compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: Reducing SDS-PAGE of preparations containing ApoE3 or ApoE4 showed approximately 70-kDa bands assigned to ApoE dimers, including ApoE-only aggregate controls, without reporting whether dimer abundance differed between isoforms.
rows.Finding quote: We observed also some higher molecular weight bands of ~70 kDa in SDS-PAGE lanes, as shown in Figure 4A, corresponding to S100A9 aggregated with ApoE isoforms. These bands correspond to the dimer of ApoE as they appeared in the lanes, which contain only ApoE aggregates (Figure 4A).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (relative ApoE dimer abundance unresolved; ApoE dimers reported in the isoform experiment)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free recombinant human ApoE3 and ApoE4 preparations, with lipid-free and DOPC/cholesterol-lipidated samples included. Fig 4A examines samples after 70 h at 42 °C in PBS using reducing SDS-PAGE and Coomassie staining; co-incubation samples contained 50 μM S100A9 and 2 μM ApoE. ApoE-only controls were also loaded. The text does not resolve the dimer signal by every lipidation/isoform lane.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 adheres more tightly to some recycling receptors than APOE3, impeding recycling.

rows.Finding description: Human apoE3 and apoE4 particles showed no reproducible difference in the ligand-blot binding pattern on murine Neuro-2a membrane proteins. The authors reported this qualitative comparison without a statistical test.
rows.Finding quote: The prominent apoE-binding bands had apparent molecular masses of 280, 212, 206, 167, and 147 kDa. No reproducible differences were seen between apoE3 and apoE4 particles.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (no change in detectable binding to Neuro-2a membrane proteins)
rows.Experimental system: Human apoE3 and apoE4 particles were immunoaffinity-purified from conditioned medium of stably transfected murine Neuro-2a neuroblastoma clones 1B and 1E4A, respectively. Target membrane proteins came from Neuro-2a cells incubated for 16 h in serum-free basal medium with N2 supplements. Nonheated, nonreduced membrane proteins (200 micrograms) were separated by 4–8% SDS-PAGE and transferred to nitrocellulose. Ligand blots were incubated with apoE particles at 1 microgram/ml for 1 h at room temperature in buffer containing 2 mM CaCl2, followed by anti-apoE detection. Companion receptor blots suggested LDLR, gp330, and LR8B/apoER2 as candidate binding proteins. This was an immobilized-protein binding assay; affinity, endosomal dissociation, and receptor recycling were not measured.
